text:
Temporal attention offers a plausible way to distinguish current intent from persistent interests without assuming every older interaction matters less. [TemProxRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784) combines absolute and relative temporal/positional embeddings in self-attention, alongside temporal-proximity contrastive learning. Earlier foundations remain directly relevant: [TiSASRec](https://jiachengli1995.github.io/files/wsdm20.pdf) models pairwise interaction intervals separately from sequence positions; [Déjà vu](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.00741) learns contextualized temporal kernels that adjust historical relevance using both content and elapsed time. These support learned temporal dependence, but do not establish gains for this pinned BERT4Rec benchmark.

Recent BERT4Rec-specific work includes a [2026 session-enhancement model](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44163-026-01554-z) combining a bidirectional long-history encoder, time-aware session attention, and jointly optimized gating. Its continuous decay explicitly favors freshness, so it provides weaker motivation for an unconstrained temporal bias. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) also examines excessive emphasis on recent interactions, reinforcing the need to distinguish useful temporal structure from imposed recency.

Experimental implication, rather than an established result: retain one BERT4Rec network per category and compare zero-initialized, learned per-head relative-position biases against timestamp-interval biases, optionally conditioned on sequence content. Leave bias values unconstrained so older relevant events can receive greater weight. Preserve masked-target training and appended-mask inference; derive temporal inputs only from observed histories, never held-out target timestamps. Select using macro validation HR@10; the supplied sensitivity results establish no preferred recency direction.
